client: I got a rejection letter from my dream university last week, and I honestly haven't been able to stop thinking about it since. It feels like no matter how hard I worked or how much I wanted it, it just wasn't enough — like I'm not enough. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help, and I'm really glad you did. That rejection clearly cut deep — not just as a disappointment about a school, but as a message you've started to believe about your own worth, and that's such a painful place to sit with. I'm curious — when you hear yourself say "I'm not enough," what does that voice sound like, and is it one you'd use with someone you care about who went through the same thing?

client: Honestly, that question kind of stopped me for a second, because no — I would never say that to a friend. I'd probably tell them that one rejection doesn't define them and that they worked really hard. But when it comes to myself, it just feels different, like the rules don't apply the same way, and I'm not sure why that is.
therapist: What you just noticed is really significant — you already *know* the compassionate truth, you just haven't been able to direct it inward yet, and that gap between how we treat ourselves versus others is something so many people struggle with. It's almost like there's a different, harsher rulebook reserved just for you, and it's worth wondering where that rulebook came from and who actually wrote it. What do you think would happen if, just as an experiment, you tried speaking to yourself the way you'd speak to that friend — even if it feels a little uncomfortable or undeserved at first?

client: I think I'd probably feel like I was lying to myself, honestly — like I'd be saying words that sound nice but don't actually match what I believe deep down. It's hard to explain, but telling a friend "one rejection doesn't define you" feels true when I say it to them, but if I tried to say it to myself it would just feel hollow, like I'm trying to trick myself into feeling better. I guess I'm skeptical that just changing the way I talk to myself is going to change what I actually feel.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely valid — just repeating positive phrases without really believing them can feel hollow, and that's not what we're going for here. What's worth exploring is *why* the same words feel true for your friend but not for you — because that difference isn't about the words, it's about a deeper belief you hold that somehow the rule doesn't apply to you specifically, and that belief itself is worth examining. What's the evidence, when you really look at it honestly, that *you* are the exception — that this rejection actually does define your worth in a way it wouldn't for someone else?

client: When you put it that way, I can't actually come up with solid evidence that I'm the exception — it's more like a feeling than a fact, which I guess is kind of the point you're making. But I think part of me feels like my situation is different because I put so much of myself into this, more than I've ever put into anything, so the rejection feels more personal than it would for someone else. Like the harder you try, the more a failure means about you — which I'm saying out loud and already kind of hearing how that might not be logical.
therapist: You just did something really powerful — you caught your own thinking mid-sentence and questioned it yourself, which shows real insight. That belief, "the harder I try, the more a failure means about me," is actually the opposite of how most people would logically frame effort — if anything, pouring yourself into something says something meaningful *about* you, regardless of the outcome. What do you think that enormous effort you put in actually reflects about who you are as a person?

client: I guess it reflects that I care deeply about things and I'm willing to work hard for what I want, which... aren't bad qualities to have. But there's still this part of me that feels like caring that much and still not getting it is almost worse — like it would've hurt less if I hadn't tried so hard. I'm not sure how to sit with the fact that I gave everything and it still didn't work out.
therapist: What you just named - that caring deeply and trying hard are genuinely good qualities - is really worth holding onto, even when it doesn't feel like enough right now. The pain you're feeling isn't a sign that trying was a mistake; it's actually a reflection of how much capacity you have for commitment and passion, which will matter enormously in whatever comes next. I'm wondering — if you imagine yourself a few years from now looking back at this moment, what do you think you'd want the version of you sitting here today to know?

client: I think that future version of me would probably want me to know that this wasn't the end, that life kept going and things worked out somehow even if they looked different than I planned. But honestly, it's really hard to access that perspective right now because the rejection still feels so fresh and so loud that the future feels kind of abstract and far away. I want to believe that version of me exists, but right now it's like trying to see something through fog.
therapist: That fog is real, and it makes complete sense that it's hard to see through it just one week out from something that hurt this much — you're not failing at healing, you're just still in the early, raw part of it. But notice that you *could* imagine that future self, even faintly, which means some part of you already believes they exist, even if you can't fully feel it yet. What might it look like to be just a little gentle with yourself this week — not to force the fog to lift, but to give yourself permission to still be in it?

client: I think being gentle with myself sounds good in theory, but I'm not totally sure what that actually looks like in practice — like, does it mean letting myself feel bad without judging it, or does it mean doing things that comfort me, because those feel like different things and I'm not sure I know how to do either right now. Part of me worries that giving myself permission to be in the fog might just mean I stay there longer, like I'll use it as an excuse to not move forward. I don't want to wallow, but I also don't want to keep beating myself up — I just don't know how to find the middle ground.
therapist: You've actually just described the middle ground really well — it lives right between "pushing yourself to be over it" and "letting the fog become permanent," and the fact that you're already thinking about both sides shows you're not someone who's going to wallow. Being gentle with yourself can actually include both things you named — letting yourself feel the sadness without piling judgment on top of it, *and* doing small things that care for you — and neither one is an excuse to stop moving forward, they're actually what makes moving forward possible. What's one small thing, even something tiny, that has felt caring or comforting to you in hard times before — something that didn't require the fog to be gone first?

client: There's this one thing where I make tea and sit by the window without my phone — I used to do it sometimes in the mornings and it always felt like a small quiet moment that was just mine. But I haven't done it since the rejection letter came, which I guess is kind of telling. I'm a little worried that if I sit in that quiet now, all the thoughts about the rejection will just get louder, but maybe that's not necessarily a reason to avoid it.
therapist: That small ritual sounds genuinely beautiful, and the fact that you've been avoiding it since the rejection is really telling — it's like you've been protecting yourself from your own quiet, which makes sense when the thoughts feel loud and scary. But here's something worth considering: the thoughts are already there whether you're in the quiet or not, and that window-and-tea moment might actually give them a gentler, safer container than the busy noise you've been using to outrun them. What do you think it would feel like to try it just once this week — not to solve anything or feel better, just to give yourself that small quiet moment that's yours again?

client: I think I could probably try it once — it feels like a small enough thing that I can't really talk myself out of it the way I might with something bigger. But I'm also aware that I'm saying that now in this conversation where I feel a little more grounded, and I'm not sure if I'll actually follow through when I'm alone and the rejection is sitting heavy again. I guess the honest answer is I want to try, and I'm just hoping that wanting to is enough to actually do it.
therapist: Wanting to try *is* a real and meaningful starting point — it's not nothing, it's actually the seed of the whole thing. One small way to bridge the gap between this grounded moment and that harder one is to make the intention concrete now, like deciding a specific morning this week when you'll make the tea, so that future-you doesn't have to make the decision from inside the fog. And if you do sit down with that tea and the thoughts get loud, can you be curious about that too — not as something going wrong, but as part of what it means to gently show up for yourself right now?

client: Okay, I think I can commit to Thursday morning — that feels specific enough to be real but far enough away that I'm not dreading it right now. The idea of being curious about the loud thoughts instead of just trying to survive them is interesting, though I'm not sure I'll actually be able to pull that off in the moment — it sounds like something that's easier to say here than to do when I'm sitting there alone with it all. But I think I'm willing to try, and maybe that's what I keep coming back to — just being willing, even when I'm not sure.
therapist: Thursday morning feels like a real, meaningful commitment, and "just being willing, even when I'm not sure" is honestly one of the most honest and courageous things you can bring to hard moments — it's not about having it all figured out, it's about showing up anyway. You came into this conversation doubting it would change anything, and look at where you've moved to — not to a place where everything is fixed, but to a place where you're a little more curious and a little less alone with it all. How are you feeling right now, compared to when you first started talking today?
